post_title: How many Washington dairy herds will WSDA have confirmed H5N1-positive as of November 12, 2026?

question.title: How many Washington dairy herds will WSDA have confirmed H5N1-positive as of November 12, 2026?
question.description:
Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) has circulated in US dairy cattle since March 2024, when it was first confirmed in Texas; detections have since occurred in herds in 19 states. US officials confirmed 917 dairy herds in 2024 and 171 in 2025, and about 93 so far in 2026 (CIDRAP, October 2026). Washington state had no confirmed HPAI detections in cattle before October 2026 — WSDA and Washington State University had run more than 7,000 surveillance tests that all came back negative.

That changed on October 8, 2026, when USDA's National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL) confirmed H5N1 in two Yakima County dairy herds, the state's first known cases in cattle. Genetic sequencing showed the cow-adapted B3.13 genotype that has circulated in dairy cattle since spring 2024. The outbreak then escalated very quickly, and the Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) publishes a running, date-stamped table of confirmed H5N1 detections in Washington cattle. As of October 29, 2026 that table totals 34 dairy herds: 33 in Yakima County and 1 in Benton County. The progression by the table's confirmation dates has been 10/08 (2 herds), 10/15 (1), 10/16 (5), 10/21 (1), 10/23 (17 Yakima + 1 Benton), 10/27 (3), 10/29 (4) — i.e. 2 herds on October 8, 9 by October 21, 27 by October 23, 34 by October 29. Reporting is lumpy: large batches (17 herds dated October 23) reflect testing surges and retrospective confirmation rather than same-day infections.

The Benton County herd (which the table dates October 23 but which WSDA announced in a news release on October 26) marked spread to a second county, and a Washington dairy worker has also tested positive for H5N1 with mild symptoms. State veterinarian Amber Itle said on October 29 that "the virus is moving fast … despite all the efforts that we've done within containment," while emphasizing that the risk to the general public remains very low. Affected herds are quarantined and required to follow strict biosecurity measures.

Scale context matters for forecasting the ceiling. Washington has roughly 300 licensed dairy operations and about 270,000 dairy cows. Yakima County has the state's largest concentration of dairy cows — more than half of state milk production — with about 41 licensed facilities regulated under the state's Dairy Nutrient Management Program in a 2023 count (additional licensed dairies exist outside that program), so the 33 herds already confirmed in Yakima could represent a large share of the county's licensed dairies or a more modest share, depending on the true denominator. Whether the count keeps climbing by a few herds per day, decelerates as quarantines bite and local susceptible herds are exhausted, or accelerates into neighbouring Benton, Franklin and Grant county dairies is the central forecasting question.

Source note: news reporting of the state count has run ahead of USDA's federal "HPAI Confirmed Cases in Livestock" dashboard, which is updated each weekday and, on October 27, had not yet reflected the jump from 9 to 27 herds reported by the state. WSDA's table records detections that WSDA describes in its news releases as confirmed by USDA NVSL, and it is the most current and granular public count, so it is used here as the resolution source.

question.resolution_criteria: This question resolves to the sum of the "NUMBER OF HERDS" column across all dated detection rows with a "TYPE" of "Dairy" in the "2026 table of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 cases in Washington cattle" on the Washington State Department of Agriculture's [HPAI (H5N1) in Cattle page](https://agr.wa.gov/departments/animals-livestock-and-pets/avian-health/avian-influenza/hpai-(h5n1)-in-cattle-producer-resources), counting only rows whose "DATE CONFIRMED" is on or before November 12, 2026, with the table read as it appears on November 13, 2026 (Pacific Time). Each herd is counted once, by its date confirmed; if WSDA later splits, consolidates or removes rows, herds confirmed on or before November 12, 2026 still count toward the total. For scale, that same table summed to 34 herds as of October 29, 2026, which would resolve as 34. If the WSDA page or its table is unavailable, [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) reporting WSDA's cumulative statewide count of H5N1-confirmed Washington dairy herds will be used.
question.fine_print: Rows added to the table after the November 13, 2026 reading — including any carrying a date confirmed on or before November 12, 2026 — do not change the resolution. Non-dairy cattle rows are excluded, and detections in any Washington county count toward the total.
